title: This world is hau
hook: na na na, hey hey. songs everywhere carry syllables that mean nothing. the Sama Veda's chants have them too, and the Chandogya gives them a world
carry: upasana: seeing the whole world in the rite
tomorrow: what does the song rest on?

segments.voice: Yesterday, still in the Sama Veda: prana, the breath evil couldn't pierce. Every sense went both ways, and only the life-breath could carry the chant.

Na na na na. Hey hey. Ooh, la la. Plenty of songs have a stretch where the words run out and the singer keeps going anyway. Nobody looks those syllables up. And yet a crowd of strangers will sing them back, louder than the verses. Sama Veda chant has syllables like that too, sounds slipped between the words of the verse to carry the melody. A reader could skip them as filler. The Chandogya Upanishad doesn't. Today: the sounds between the words.
screen: `NA NA NA. HEY HEY.` → `NOT IN ANY DICTIONARY.` → `THE SOUNDS BETWEEN THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: When a verse becomes a saman, a Sama Veda chant, the words don't stay as they were. Vowels stretch. Syllables repeat. And between them come extra sounds, with names like hau and hai and auhoyi. These are stobhas. On their own they don't mean anything the way a word does; they're there for the song. Then the Chandogya gives the stobhas the world. In paraphrase: this world is the sound hau. The wind is hai. The moon is atha. And it goes on down a list, pairing chant-sounds with fire, with the sun, with breath, with food. So the sounds a hurried listener would call filler, the Upanishad treats as the places where the whole world comes into the song. This is a way of worship the Upanishads teach again and again, called upasana, literally a sitting near: meditating on one part of a rite as something greater. The singer doesn't only sound hau; he holds this world in it. Readers take it more than one way. Some hear a meditation, a way to keep the whole world in mind while chanting. Some hear a point about sound itself: in Hindu practice a sacred sound can matter even where it carries no dictionary meaning, and Vedic chanters still learn every syllable by ear and keep it exact. Either way, the Chandogya refuses to throw the small sounds away. In this teaching, nothing in a rite is too small to hold the world.
screen: `STRETCHED, REPEATED, FILLED IN.` · `STOBHAS: HAU, HAI, AUHOYI.` · `THIS WORLD IS HAU. THE WIND IS HAI.` · then, large: `UPASANA: THE WHOLE WORLD IN A SMALL SOUND.`

segments.voice: On the out-breath let a soft open sound come, like haa or hau, quiet enough that no one else hears, just a sound with no meaning. On the next breaths make the same sound and let it hold one thing each time, the ground under you, the air in the room; if silence suits the place you're in, make the sound inside. If you pray, let it be prayer.
The Sama Veda as song. In the chant, small sounds called stobhas carry the melody, and the Chandogya meditates on them as the world: upasana. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: upasana, seeing the whole world in the rite. Even in the small sounds. Same time tomorrow.
